article.title: Why I joined Tempest
article.author: Keegan O'Brien
article.content: I’ m writing this message from Belfast, Northern Ireland. I’m on a solo trip around the country, and it’s been absolutely stunning. If you haven’t been to Ireland, I highly recommend making the trip! Today, I visited the James Connolly Museum, and the experience moved me to share some photos and brief reflections about my political life. These past seven-plus years since the dissolution of the International Socialist Organization have been a politically challenging time for me as a revolutionary socialist, as I know they have been for many others. At times, I still feel like I’ve lost my political home and anchor, struggling to stay afloat, make sense of what’s happening in the world, and figure out what comes next. In spite of that, I’m incredibly grateful to be part of the Tempest Collective and to be committed to carrying forward the tradition of revolutionary socialism from below with all of you. My convictions in the politics of working-class self-emancipation, anti-imperialism, international solidarity, the struggle against oppression, and the need for revolutionary organization remain firmer today than at any point in my political life. Like many comrades, I have questions about what the future holds and where we go from here. But I’m proud to be part of an organization where we can figure that out together. We stand on the shoulders of giants and come from a living, breathing political tradition built through the sacrifice and dedication of countless people over decades and centuries. Walking through the museum today and touring the murals throughout the city reminded me that our project is so much greater than any one person or organization. We stand on the shoulders of giants and come from a living, breathing political tradition built through the sacrifice and dedication of countless people over decades and centuries—people who have struggled for a socialist future free of oppression and exploitation, often under circumstances far more grim and difficult than those we face today. It is a tradition built by generations of dedicated revolutionaries who refused to accept the limitations of what was considered possible, and who remained committed to the possibility of a society radically different from the one they inherited. James Connolly’s life and politics are a powerful example of that tradition: They are rooted in working-class self-emancipation, internationalism, anti-imperialism, and the conviction that the liberation of the working class could not be separated from the liberation of the oppressed. Mural in Belfast depicting solidarity between Irish and Palestinian prisoners of war. Image credit: author. After decades of neoliberalism, characterized by working-class retreat and the decline of Left and socialist organizations, it has been inspiring and hopeful to see new generations of people radicalize against the brutality of capitalism and become open to the basic ideas of socialism and working-class politics. In many ways, it is easier today to be a socialist than at any point in my political life. At the same time, being a revolutionary socialist can still be profoundly isolating and difficult, making it easy to question: What am I doing here? Is all our time and effort in this project really worth it? Much of what remains of the socialist Left in the U.S. has either lost sight of or rejected a project of revolutionary transformation. Being part of Tempest reminds me that there are still many of us, albeit a minority, who have refused to let go of that vision. The growth and electoral success of DSA is inspiring and hopeful, but it does not overcome the structural barriers of an electoral road to socialism. Nor does electoral success, by itself, fundamentally alter the balance of class forces or necessarily rebuild the self-organization, political consciousness, and combativity of our class—which we know are the basis for a socialist future. The work we are doing in Tempest, alongside the efforts of comrades and organizations across the revolutionary Left …is part of that longer history and contributes to the ongoing process of reconstituting and rebuilding a rich and vibrant revolutionary movement. Walking around the streets of Belfast today, seeing the incredible murals painted throughout the city, and learning about the life of James Connolly has reminded me that nothing in this world stays fixed forever. Our movements, and this tradition of revolutionary socialism, have gone through many ebbs and flows—periods of tremendous success followed by bleak and difficult setbacks. The work we are doing in Tempest, alongside the efforts of comrades and organizations across the revolutionary Left to develop working-class cadre, advance Marxism as a distinct ideological and political current for understanding and transforming the world, and to rebuild the broader infrastructures of dissent and resistance, is part of that longer history and contributes to the ongoing process of reconstituting and rebuilding a rich and vibrant revolutionary movement, however modest or small these efforts may feel today. We may not see the fruits of that work immediately, or even in our own lifetimes, but by rebuilding this tradition today, we are planting the seeds for the struggles and victories of tomorrow. Mural in Belfast for the Workers Party. Image credit: author. Connolly understood this too, and in his 1909 pamphlet Socialism Made Easy , he captures the revolutionary conviction that what seems impractical in one historical conjuncture may become possible in another—and that our task is to prepare for that moment, even when the balance of class forces and capitalism’s efforts to narrow the collective horizons of our class make the prospects for revolutionary change seem remote: Revolution is never practical—until the hour of the Revolution strikes. Then it alone is practical, and all the efforts of the conservatives and compromisers become the most futile and visionary of human imaginings. For that hour let us work, think and hope; for that hour let us pawn our present ease in hopes of a glorious redemption; for that hour let us prepare the hosts of labor with intelligence sufficient to laugh at the nostrums dubbed practical by our slave-lords, practical for the perpetuation of our slavery; for that supreme crisis of human history, let us watch, like sentinels, with weapons ever ready, remembering always that there can be no dignity in Labor until Labor knows no master. I’m grateful to be on this journey with all of you, fighting for a world where, in Connolly’s words, labor knows no master. Being part of the socialist movement has helped make this life one worth living. We still have a world to win, and I’m committed to fighting for it alongside you. In comradeship and solidarity, Keegan Opinions expressed in signed articles do not necessarily represent the views of the editors or the Tempest Collective.
